articles.title: Rochdale Road East Reopens After Crash Outside Heywood Cemetery
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Road East, located outside Heywood Cemetery, has reopened following a crash that closed the road in both directions earlier today.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Road East, outside Heywood Cemetery, has reopened after being closed in both directions following a crash this afternoon.

Emergency services responded to the incident, which resulted in significant delays for motorists.

The road was closed for several hours while the scene was cleared and investigations were conducted.

Drivers are advised to remain cautious as traffic returns to normal.

articles.title: New grassroots club Heywood Hurricanes FC appeals for raffle prizes to keep football free for every child
articles.excerpt: A brand-new junior football club with one simple goal - making the game accessible to every child regardless of family finances - is asking local businesses to donate raffle prizes.
articles.content_html:
A brand-new grassroots football club in Heywood is appealing to local businesses for raffle prizes as it works to keep the game affordable for every child who wants to play.

Heywood Hurricanes FC has been set up with what it calls one simple goal: to make football accessible for every child. The club says every young player deserves the opportunity to enjoy football, make friends, build confidence and be part of a team - regardless of their family's financial circumstances.

Rather than leaning on sponsorship from the outset, the club is trying to raise funds itself. "As a brand-new club, we're under no illusion that sponsorships are easy to come by," the Hurricanes said. "We know local businesses receive lots of requests, and we completely understand that not everyone is in a position to help financially."

Over the coming weeks the club will hold a raffle to help ease the financial burden on its families and keep costs as low as possible for players. It is asking whether any local businesses would be willing to donate a prize - a voucher, gift hamper, experience, service, or anything else. Every donation, big or small, the club says, will make a genuine difference.

The appeal comes at a time when many families are struggling with the cost of children's sport. Subs, kit, boots and travel add up quickly, and money is increasingly the reason children drop out of the game. By fundraising to keep its own costs down, the Hurricanes hope no child in Heywood is priced off the pitch.

"Your generosity will help us provide opportunities for children to play the game they love without additional financial pressure on their parents, especially at a time when many families are finding things incredibly tough," the club said.

Anyone who would like to support Heywood Hurricanes, or who knows someone who might be able to help, can get in touch by messaging the club's Facebook page.
articles.legal_disclaimer: This article is based on an appeal published by Heywood Hurricanes FC. Rochdale Daily has no involvement in the raffle; anyone wishing to donate should contact the club directly.

articles.title: Planning Approved for Seven-Bedroom Home at Former Coronation Street Star's Residence
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for a seven-bedroom luxury home at the site of Julie Goodyear’s former residence, following a series of controversial proposals.
articles.content_html:
A planning application to convert the former home of Coronation Street star Julie Goodyear into a seven-bedroom luxury house has been approved by Rochdale Council. The site, located at Primrose Hill Farm on Rochdale Road East, has been the subject of controversy and confusion regarding its future.

Dr Liaqat Malik, the new owner, submitted the application after construction work began without a valid planning application, prompting a temporary stop notice from the council on February 20. This led to protests based on false rumours that the property would be converted into a house of multiple occupation for immigrants.

During the planning committee meeting on August 5, no objectors attended to contest the proposal. Dr Malik clarified that previous plans submitted to building control were mistakenly filed, which contributed to the misunderstandings surrounding the site. The approved plans include three en-suite bedrooms on the ground floor, along with a kitchen, dining room, reception area, cinema room, and a family bathroom. The first floor will feature four additional en-suite bedrooms and a lounge, with provisions for parking seven cars.

The site has seen several changing applications in recent months, including proposals for a 15-bed house of multiple occupation and various configurations of apartments and bed and breakfast accommodations. The latest approved plan marks a significant shift towards a single-family luxury residence, with further details on the conversion of stables into a garage and recreational areas.

articles.content_html:
Education Minister and local MP Paul Waugh visited the Derby Street Best Start Family Hub in Heywood this morning. During his visit, he was introduced to the various services provided by the hub in collaboration with multi-agency partners.

The hub aims to support local families with children, offering a range of resources and assistance tailored to their needs. Waugh's visit highlights the government's commitment to early years support and community engagement.

Local families benefit from the initiatives at the hub, which focus on improving child development and well-being. The collaborative efforts of various agencies aim to create a supportive environment for parents and children alike.

This visit underscores the importance of community resources in fostering healthy family dynamics and ensuring children receive the best possible start in life.

articles.title: Heywood Sports Village Hosts Annual White Ribbon Football Tournament
articles.excerpt: Teams from various organisations participated in the annual White Ribbon Football Tournament at Heywood Sports Village, promoting awareness and unity.
articles.content_html:
A football tournament took place yesterday at Heywood Sports Village, featuring teams from across the council and partner organisations. The event was part of the annual White Ribbon initiative, which aims to raise awareness about domestic violence and promote healthy relationships.

More than 50 players participated in the tournament, showcasing their skills on the pitch. Before the matches commenced, all participants made a pledge in support of the White Ribbon campaign, which encourages men to take a stand against violence towards women.

The tournament not only provided an opportunity for friendly competition but also aimed to foster community spirit and collaboration among various local organisations. It served as a platform to highlight the importance of addressing domestic violence issues within the community.

The event was well-received, with participants and supporters alike expressing their commitment to the cause. Such initiatives are crucial in promoting awareness and encouraging positive change in society.

articles.title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
articles.excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
articles.content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

articles.title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
articles.excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

articles.title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
articles.excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

articles.title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

articles.title: White Ribbon Football Tournament returns to Rochdale for 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced the return of its annual White Ribbon Football Tournament, bringing together teams from across the authority to promote the campaign to end violence against women and girls.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that its annual White Ribbon Football Tournament will return on Tuesday 4 August 2026, bringing together teams from across the council in support of the White Ribbon campaign.

Before kick-off, participating teams will take the White Ribbon pledge, reaffirming their commitment to helping end violence against women and girls.

The council is a White Ribbon accredited organisation and says the tournament has been organised entirely by members of staff in their own time to raise awareness of the campaign and encourage conversations around preventing abuse and violence.

Residents are encouraged to attend and cheer on the teams throughout the day. While places in the tournament itself are limited, spectators are welcome.

The tournament takes place at Heywood Sports Village on Tuesday 4 August 2026, and spectators are welcome.

The White Ribbon campaign works to engage men and boys in preventing violence against women and girls by promoting positive attitudes, respectful relationships and challenging harmful behaviours.

articles.title: Cloud Gardener Jason Williams to host wellbeing gardening evening in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Television gardening expert Jason Williams will visit Heywood this month for a free community wellbeing event exploring the benefits of container gardening, hosted by Heywood in Bloom as part of the Great Heywood Gathering.
articles.content_html:
Residents are being invited to discover how gardening can support wellbeing when television presenter and horticultural expert Jason Williams visits Heywood later this month for a free community event. Organised by Heywood in Bloom as part of the Great Heywood Gathering programme, the evening will explore how container gardening can improve both physical and mental wellbeing while helping people make the most of even the smallest outdoor spaces.

The event, titled 'Grow Well', will take place on Wednesday, 12 August, from 6.30pm until 9.30pm at Corcoran Close Community Room, Heywood. Organisers say refreshments will be provided free of charge, giving local residents an opportunity to meet others from the community while learning practical gardening techniques from one of the country's best-known horticultural communicators.

Jason Williams, widely known as the 'Cloud Gardener', has built a large following through his work promoting accessible gardening and encouraging people to grow flowers, fruit and vegetables in urban environments. His approach focuses on making gardening achievable for everyone, regardless of the size of their garden or outdoor space, with container gardening becoming increasingly popular among people living in flats, terraces and homes with smaller gardens.

Research continues to demonstrate the benefits gardening can have for health and wellbeing. NHS-backed social prescribing schemes increasingly include community gardening projects as a way of improving mental health, reducing loneliness, encouraging gentle physical activity and strengthening social connections. Studies have also linked time spent in green spaces with reduced stress levels and improved overall wellbeing.

The event forms part of the wider Great Heywood Gathering initiative, supported through the Culture Co-op's Creative People and Places programme. The initiative aims to bring local communities together through arts, culture, wellbeing and environmental activities, encouraging more residents to become involved in projects that improve the town and strengthen neighbourhood connections.

Heywood in Bloom has played an important role in enhancing public spaces across the town through volunteer-led planting schemes, community gardening projects and environmental improvements. Working alongside residents, schools and community organisations, the group has helped transform flower beds, public spaces and neglected areas while promoting biodiversity and civic pride.

The event has been supported by Rochdale Borough Council, Your Trust, Arts Council England, The National Lottery Community Fund and Pride in Place, reflecting the collaborative approach taken to delivering community activities across the borough.

Organisers hope the evening will inspire more people to discover the benefits of gardening, whether by growing flowers on a balcony, vegetables in containers or creating wildlife-friendly spaces at home. They also hope the event will encourage new volunteers to become involved with Heywood in Bloom and future environmental projects across the town.

Anyone interested in attending is encouraged to arrive in time for the 6.30pm start at Corcoran Close Community Room, OL10 4XD. With expert advice, free refreshments and a focus on community wellbeing, organisers hope the evening will leave attendees with practical ideas, new friendships and the confidence to start growing at home.
